utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue the examination of the witness, I'm informed, Mr. Ierace, that you'd like to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This morning the Prosecution and Defence met with Ms. Tournaye to discuss the sequence and dates of expert witnesses and others. As a result of that meeting, an order has been agreed and prospective dates established which take us to and including the 4th of March. However, there is an issue which the Prosecution seeks to raise. The Prosecution has until recently worked on the basis that the time sought by the Defence for examination-in-chief of expert witnesses would be utilised by way of amplification of what appears in the reports and would not go beyond that. As a result of recent correspondence from the Defence, it appears that in respect at least of one expert - and that is Professor Radinovic - the Defence had intended to tender through him certain documents which are not in his report and by inference give evidence on matters which are not in his report. Mr. President, that being the case, the Prosecution wishes to make clear that its estimates of cross-examination are based on the assumption that the time taken in chief will be utilised exclusively to amplify matters in the report. If the Defence goes beyond the contents of the report, then to that extent the Prosecution seeks equal time, pursuant to the usual Rule, and a 65 ter summary in respect of that additional non-expert evidence, together with, of course, the usual seven days' notice of exhibits -- additional exhibits to be tendered through that witness. These matters will be covered in a short-form fashion in a motion to be filed today, more specifically in relation to Dr. Radinovic. Mr. President, to the extent that any additional evidence led in chief is properly characterised as being of an expert nature, then the Prosecution objects to such evidence because it would not comply to the Rules pertaining to expert evidence within a particular field of expertise. In other words, it should be in the report duly served. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter, Mr. Ierace. It has happened also in the Prosecution case that sometimes an expert has testified as a witness. But this was under very special circumstances. And the subject matter then was -- at least the factual basis of his expert report. But perhaps we'd like to hear, perhaps not immediately, but perhaps this afternoon from you, Ms. Pilipovic, what causes you to introduce new factual evidence through an expert witness, factual evidence that would not be in -- dealt with in the -- in the expert report. We'd like to hear that from you first before further considering the matter. But perhaps we -- either you do it now immediately. That's also a possibility. But, of course, the Chamber is still very uncertain about the type of material that you wanted to introduce as new factual elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in its submission to the Chamber and my learned friends, the Defence indicated that these are documents which the Defence would like to show Mr. Radinovic as a military expert which are not annexed to the expert report, and these are military documents of the BH army which the Defence received from the Prosecution, and the expert witness had the opportunity to familiarise himself with them but did not quote them in his report. We are not challenging the authenticity of these documents, but we think that it is in the interest of justice to have a military expert explain several documents which is not included in the report but has gone through such documents and that it also would be useful to give us his interpretation of the content of these documents. So these are not new documents. This is our position. I made our submission yesterday in writing, and today at a meeting I suggested to my learned colleague -- to my learned friend to possibly discuss these documents -- which documents because -- will be shown because these documents are both in the hands of the Prosecution and Defence. In other words, these are not new military documents which are not in the possession of both the Defence and the Prosecution. But no doubt you will give us your opinion, although my learned friend, as he has said, will also respond in writing and then perhaps I will have to make some additional explanations. In our submission, we also raised an issue which is of major importance for the Defence, and that is whether every document that has been annexed to Dr. Radinovic's document is automatically considered as exhibit or do we have to tender every one of them separately, although they're included with the -- with the expert's report, and I have also indicated that matter in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, may I just make a very short comment. I do understand that if the expert has been provided with certain documents which he did not mention in his report, I can imagine that one of the questions would be did you know the existence of the document? You didn't use it, or you didn't at least mention it. Was there a specific reason for that? I mean, what is not in an expert report could be part of questioning as well. But on the other hand, that, of course, should not result in totally new grounds to be entered, a totally new area to be entered on the basis of these document, because then it certainly would have had to be in the initial report. So it's a bit difficult perhaps at this very moment without knowing how many of these documents there are and what exactly the type of questions will be, but perhaps further communication between the parties could clarify this to some extent. But Mr. Ierace, if you want to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Very briefly. Disclosure has got nothing to do with it. That's not the issue. I don't think it's a matter for the discussion between the parties. I think it's important that it be dealt with on the record because otherwise it may impact adversely on the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- At a later stage. Finally, Mr. President, might I inform you as I informed Ms. Tournaye, that in relation to Professor Cavoski where we previously indicated half an hour for cross-examination, as a result of some fresh material that's come to our attention we seek to increase that to one and a half hours and to compensate, take an hour off cross-examination time for Milan Kunjadic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In your proposal which have not yet been decided upon by the Chamber, but we'll take that into consideration. Ms. Pilipovic, today I got on my desk the appearance of next Friday of Dr. Vilicic. But that's not valid, any more, I take it on the basis of the new schedule you worked out. Yes. Then I think it would be -- Ms. Pilipovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, not Dr. Vilicic, Your Honour. I do not know which Friday you have in mind. Tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The letter of the 4th of February. And I think that's not --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's right. We made a completely new schedule today, and I believe you have been informed about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... At this very moment. I think then it would be an appropriate moment to call the witness -- to have the witness brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Knezevic. May I first remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony. Having said this, I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us, and you used, as far as I remember, the word "decisive defence." Could you explain to us what a decisive defence is and in what way it differs from just a defence.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decisive defence -- the decisive defence is a term which means defensive tasks only. That is, the troops may never undertake any offensive activities, and that would include the opening of fire before the enemy. That is, if you're only defending yourself, only if you see the movements of adversary troops, then you can react. But when it comes to decisive defence, you open fire only when the enemy attacks you. And that kind of defence also presumes holding the positions at all cost. So this is the defence which does not include any form of retreat, which was important for us since beyond the front line trenches there were women and children who were beyond the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean that in responding to an attack from the opposite side that you would defend and in this defence gain some terrain?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Never. You don't advance. The decisive defence means staying in the trenches, never abandoning the trenches -- or rather, never retreating from the positions taken, either forward or backward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was the decisive defence, are you aware of -- I don't know whether you have knowledge of it. But that would be the general line in the SRK or was that just in your unit that you would have such a decisive defence operational?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that it was applied in our unit. I really wasn't in -- I really couldn't know what was done in other units, in other brigades of the corps. I simply had no way of coming by such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you now tell me the difference between defence -- because if you respond, if fire is opened at you, and if you try to keep your positions, not moving forward, not moving backwards, many people would call that a defence. What now is the difference between a decisive defence and what many people would call defence?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I'll repeat. The decisive defence is neither launching a counter-offensive nor a retreat. So there is no counter-attack nor retreat, regardless of how things unfold on the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May the witness be shown document D1453.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read paragraph 1 of that document. And could perhaps the -- first the original be put on the ELMO. And perhaps just under it, the translation of paragraph 1 so that everyone can follow it. So paragraph 1 on top of the ELMO, and then just under it the English translation. Yes. Perhaps if the original one should have moved up a tiny little bit, upwards, even more, a bit more. Have you read paragraph 1, witness? General Galic, have you been able to recognise the document that has been discussed before? Could we then zoom in on the English translation of paragraph 1. That's not paragraph 1. Paragraph 1 is just blow where the number "1" appears. There. Yes. Having read this, you see that the order for a decisive defence is here combined with improving operative positions and even with liberation and reaching important parts of the town apparently not at that moment under the control of the Bosnian Serb army. Having read this, may I ask you again if this would change anything in your answer as to what a decisive defence might be, compared to a defence?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you what the decisive defence meant in our unit. What was meant by this order -- I mean, really, I don't know this document. I see what it says here, but I know what we knew and what the order decisive defence meant to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. The documents may be returned to the witness [sic]. Could then the witness be shown a document which would have number C4. Could it be put on the ELMO. Could you please take the pointer, Mr. Knezevic. Look carefully at this map. And point at the precise position of your mortar unit, where it was located exactly. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Could we perhaps zoom in on the part of the map the witness -- Yes. Could you please point at it as precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please mark that position with a red pen.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Do you want some number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You may just put a cross there, a red cross. The exact location of your mortar unit.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday you told us that the confrontation line from where you were -- well, could you please repeat how -- at what distance the confrontation line were from your mortar position. No. You said -- what distance? You gave us distances yesterday. You don't have to point at the map at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 1.000 metres, 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was your first answer. And then later you said 100 to 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the distance between the two front lines, the front lines of the two parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you then tell us: If you said 1 kilometre, 1.000 metres, would that be to your side of the confrontation line or would that be to the opposite side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said 1.000 metres beyond the front line. And I meant our side, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You meant your side. So that would be 11 to 14 hundred metres from the other side of the confrontation line. Would that be correct, correct testimony?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain this. Yes. If the line were straight. You see, but we did not operate only in relation to a straight line. At times our artillery position was more than 2 kilometres from our front lines, because our line was not straight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did the line change in all areas, or just in a certain area?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, the line did not change at all sometime from June when we had dug our trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're talking about June 1992?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you point at where exactly the military observers were. Could you first point at it on the map.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put a cross there and the letters "MO" for "military observer."

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation. Were the observers there during the whole period you were a member of this mortar crew?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like this: They were stationed at Rajlovac. And as a matter of fact, they came from time to time. For a while they merely visited at all the artillery positions and then for a while they were there all the time. I mean, in the -- in our brigade's area. But I really don't know whether they were observers or UNPROFOR soldiers. I really don't know. But -- and they were stationed there. But they did not live there, UNPROFOR observers, they only had their position there. But they were quartered in the houses of the locals in the village of Radava, the other observers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the village of what, you said?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village Radava, the one that I lived in too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be shown Exhibit PC742. Could the centre of the map be put on the ELMO. Mr. Knezevic, you see that there's a spot indicated on the map near the village of Radava, which is L12. Could that have been the position where the UN people were stationed?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN members lived in private houses. They didn't live in just one private house all the time. I think they paid something to some people, and they would change these houses. I don't know whether they were dissatisfied or why. So it's not impossible that they lived for a certain period of time in this house, you know. But this isn't a position from which they owned or a position from which they could have observed anything in the village of Radava. Nothing can be observed in the village of Radava as far as the front is concerned, especially not from this position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say there was no observation post on the point indicated by L11?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't have been here, at this site where it's drawn, or else it hasn't been marked precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did I understand your testimony well that you said that at the point where the military observers were close to your position, that they were not there on a permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were never there all day long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were they there every day?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they came every day. When they were billeted in -- when they were stationed in Radava then they came every day to that observation post of theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. During the full period of September 1992 until September 1993, when you were at that position?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not sure whether it was throughout the entire period, because for a certain period of time they were in Rajlovac and they visited areas. But I'm not quite sure when they did this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then my next question is about mortars being fired. Yesterday you told us that when you fired your first shell, it might, well, not immediately hit the target but could be 50 metres away from what you intended to target. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the initial shots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how many shells would you usually have to fire until you would hit the target? Yesterday you said four. Was that the normal number of shells you would have to fire in order to hit your target?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the figure four when I was speaking about the theory. But when we had already marked our targets -- you know when you have a designated target and then you fire at another target, you have certain reference points, and then you can probably hit the target with the second shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you responded to fire, how many shells would you usually need? And on the basis of what information you would adjust the mortar in order to hit the target you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the intelligence that we received from the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But -- well, let's just assume you fire one shell. Who would then tell you to fire the next one a bit further, a bit nearer, a bit more to the east, a bit more to the west, and how much?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Mr. Medic. He would give us these orders, and he received information from someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would that take between the first and the second shell and then the next?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean how much time in order to get some feedback information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you first fire, and then how much time would you need to get back the information you would need to adjust, and then how much time would you then need to prepare for the next round to be fired?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Getting back the information and preparing for the next shell or ...?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how often did it happen that you hit the target with the first shell?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we fired at these mortar targets, we didn't know whether we had hit the exact target. We didn't see their mortars under the trees. We would stop firing if the enemy stopped firing. We had no reason to fire when the enemy stopped firing. So I really don't know how to give you a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But how many shells would you fire? I mean, you -- you would fire one, and you told us that you expected the mortar to move to another place.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose mortar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear your full answer translated. Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose mortar are you referring to when you say "a mortar that was moved"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the mortar that fired at your positions, for example.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't wait for it to move. Our target was to neutralise enemy fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you moved to where the fire came from; is that ...?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't move anywhere. I don't know what you mean when you say "move."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I was not clear. No. You fired to where the fire came from.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as enemy mortars are concerned, we fired at the targets we were already aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if a mobile mortar would fire at your positions, what would you do then?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that yesterday. We didn't fire -- we couldn't return fire when they fired at us from mobile mortars because a mortar is not such a weapon that enables one to fire at a mobile target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it your instruction that whenever fire was received from an unknown firing position from the other side that you would not return fire?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only fired when we were ordered to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that was not my question. My question was that when you received fire from a position not known to you as one of the, I would say, fixed or well-known firing positions from the other part, that you were instructed not to return fire to such an unknown source of fire at the other side of the line?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. How were we to return fire if we weren't aware of the target, if we didn't know where the target was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you could not fire at such a source of fire at the other side of the lines?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether you got instructions to refrain from returning fire under such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Our instructions were to fire only when ordered to do so. If they didn't order us to fire, then we didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever receive an order to fire at a source of fire at the other side of the confrontation line that was not one of the, may I say, fixed or well-known firing positions but what might have been a mobile mortar position or I must say a position of a mobile mortar?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't receive such orders except in cases - and I can't confirm or deny this - if the mortar which was firing from the area of the bus 17 -- where the bus 17 turns around, only in these cases, because it was possible for this to happen in that case. It was near -- it was close to the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you would say that apart from perhaps firing at where bus 17 would turn, that from your unit never an order was given to return fire to a source which might have been a mobile mortar and that you never did so?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never received such an order and we never did anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then one question: If you were firing at, I would say, well-known positions -- you mentioned yesterday 50 metres that the first shell might land from the actual target. Would you consider this 50 metres as your normal distance from a target, or would you say, "Well, we did it very well when we got at the distance of only 50 metres," or would it be usually 200 or 300 metres? What would be -- in your unit, what would be the performance in respect of the first shell approximately?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to a well-known target, if there was -- if the shell fell about 200 metres away, then that would mean that there was something wrong with the mortar. This is something that doesn't happen if the mortar is functioning correctly and efforts are made to ensure that the weapon functions correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's say, in how many per cent of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cases you would -- you would achieve a distance of not more than 50 metres from your target?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of well-known targets, the percentage would be very high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be 90, 95, 85, 98? A high is -- some people think 60 is high; others might think 98 is high.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How many shots you would, on an average, need to hit your target in practice? You told us yesterday about theory, but in practice on an average.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually we fired about a case. That would be four shells. And then after that the enemy would stop firing. Our aim was to make sure that fire ceased, but we usually didn't know whether we had hit the target or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you usually would fire four shells?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually four, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answers. I have no further questions to you. Is there any need to ask questions on the basis of -- Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Knezevic, yesterday in response to a question from Judge Nieto-Navia you said that in December, the new year and Christmas -- in 1992/1993, you said you spent that period at home.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said I was at home for Christmas and I celebrated the new year with my friends on Pale. That's not at home. And in the first case it wasn't at home either. It was my grandmother's home. I wasn't at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So that means that you were in the area of the positions of your brigade.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We missed that last answer. Could you please repeat your last answer, Mr. Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, now it appears in writing. Yes, please proceed. I see that your answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, yesterday you also said that you used various charges. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from Judge Nieto-Navia, you said that you used various charges.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I asked for me to be provided with the transcript. At the time I didn't have the transcript on the screen. And the question I was put was whether I knew what a charge was, and I found that very strange. It was an odd question. That's what I heard through the headphones, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what a mortar charge is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the question was: How many charges did you use when firing? And after that I asked: Well, do you know what is a charge? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there's no point in talking about various forms of charges. The M74 mortar has six identical charges. And depending on the distance of the target, which is determined by the elevation of the barrel but also by the number of charges that are used. This charge propels the shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us about additional charges?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The M74 has six regular kinds of charges.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about additional charges?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The M74 shell doesn't have any additional charges, or I didn't have any, at least. The charges are identical. There are six identical charges.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Nieto-Navia has one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I cannot follow you about the charges. Yesterday you said, and today as well, that the number of charges depends on the use you are giving to the shell. It depends on the distance and so on. You have six charges. All the shells are fired with six charges or sometimes one, two, three?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the distance of the target. And with regard to this distance, you have to adapt the elevation of the barrel and also the charge. You have to adapt it to the distance. The angle of the barrel has to be as great as possible for certain distances -- for very great distances, you use as many charges as possible. You can't use a lot of charges if the distance is not great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So you use sometimes, let's say, two or three, sometimes four, sometimes five, sometimes six charges.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, between two and six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you also one clarification. You said between two and six. Did you ever use one charge?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That would have been too risky. One charge is used if the mortar is very close to one's own lines. It's used for very short distances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would use not less than two charges.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you say using two charges and not less than two, you're speak about your own mortar battery having regard to how far your lines were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking of my mortar. I was responsible for one mortar, not for a battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. When you operate the mortar, you and the other batteries were provided with tables and charts using -- which you can calculate the appropriate number of charges, the appropriate elevation of the barrel, and the appropriate sighting of the barrel, so you could target with as much precision as possible. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Without tables, it's not possible to fire from a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So at -- let's say hypothetically, at a barrel elevation of 40 degrees, if you use one charge, it would land at a certain distance. And as you correspondingly increase the charges, the distance that the mortar lands at or impacts at increases.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you can also use a table to -- the charts or tables to change the distance using the same charge but by the elevation of the barrel.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can. You have to, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. And also, you use the charts to factor in changes in the weather and other conditions, changes -- well, if there were changes in the height, the altitude from which you fired, et cetera? When I say "et cetera," you use the tables to factor in variations, to make calculations in respect of firing the mortar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think Mr. Stamp's question doesn't arise from the questions put by the Chamber. And this is the first time we have heard the subject of tables being discussed. I think Mr. Stamp could have asked that question in the course of his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber allowed Mr. Stamp to ask questions about charts in relation to charges, which was specifically what you were asked about. But, Mr. Stamp, the weather conditions, which have not been dealt with by the Chamber have been mentioned in chief by the witness. He said that these variations also might influence. So, therefore, you could have asked that in cross-examination. The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are no further questions, then this concludes your testimony in this court, Mr. Knezevic. We all know that it's a long way to come to The Hague. We thank you very much for answering questions not only from the parties but also from the Bench. And I wish you have a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you may escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you -- Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1842, map mark by witness; Exhibit C4, map marked by witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, the documents are admitted into evidence. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness? And perhaps I should have asked the usher to bring him in right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you bring in the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, you're required by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration. The text has just been handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsman. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by counsel for the Defence. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please give us your full name, the date and place of your birth.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: My name is Sinisa Krsman. I was born on the 17th of December, 1961 in Sarajevo, municipality of Centar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, will you tell us, in 1992 where you did you live then?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: In Rajlovac, the village of Zabrdje until the 8th of May, 1992. That is, from the date of my birth until the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, we shall come back to that moment that you tell us was the 8th of May, when you stopped living there. But first I'd like to ask you, since we're talking about September 1992-August 1994, whether you can tell us if during that time you lived and were militarily engaged in the area of Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Throughout the war, I lived and was militarily engaged in the area of Rajlovac, except that from the 8th of May, I did not live in my house any longer but I was in this village of mine, that I was in my relatives' and friends' houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you were militarily engaged in the territory of Rajlovac, can you tell us if you were a member of a military formation in the area and whether there was that military formation there.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: There was no military formation in the conventional sense of the word until sometime in June or perhaps July. But when the Army of Republika Srpska was formed, by the dint of that, we all became soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska, and I had the duty of the company commander in my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you became part of the Army of Republika Srpska, can you tell us, apart from your company that you were the commander of, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. whether there were any other units in the area, and if so, how many, and whether those units were united in a larger formation.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning of the war, we were not members of an organisation. Defenders of the village, that is how you could call us. Our village was separated and we organised ourselves there. It was self-organisation to defend the village from those attacks that I will presumably talk about later on. And other villages also had people, that is, members, who lived around those houses, so we organised ourselves, but then we grew into a brigade which basically in terms of its strength was like a battalion. That is, we had three companies in that brigade -- I mean, it was called brigade, but nevertheless in terms of its strength, it was more like a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say three companies in a brigade which was only called brigade but otherwise was a battalion, can you tell us to make it quite clear whether that brigade had a name.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Since we lived in the territory of Rajlovac and that is something like an area, the brigade was called the Rajlovac Brigade. And one company was part of Brijesce and around Brijesce. Another company was the Rajlovac barracks, which was made up of the Serb refugees from the city. And the third company was my village, Zabrdje.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that as a company commander you were in a formation with other two companies, that one was in the territory of Brijesce and another in the territory of the Rajlovac barracks -- I'll come back to that so that you can explain to us better the exact locations. But could you tell us the structure of able-bodied men who were in part of, say, the Rajlovac Brigade. I understand that they were men from the areas that you have indicated.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Specifically I can tell you that in my Zabrdje company, all the fighters were from the village of Zabrdje. In other words, we had never any outsiders. I can even list all the names if it is necessary, and I will show you on the map afterwards that there is absolutely not a single individual who had come from outside. And likewise, in Brijesce, that is, in that company, the whole population of Brijesce which lived there made up that company. And in Rajlovac, the situation was somewhat more specific because the population that had been expelled from Sarajevo, the Serb population who had been expelled from Sarajevo had found shelter there and there were people from Dobrinja, Alipasino Polje, Brijesce, Buca Potok, Pofalici and so on and so forth, and they found accommodation there since that was a kind of our collective centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, after your brigade was formed and after the Army of Republika Srpska was organised - and we are talking about the time until up to August 1994 - were there any professional military in your brigade, and who was your brigade's commander?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: When we came into -- when we were formed as a unit of the Army of Republika Srpska, I personally -- or rather, all of us, we were not particularly interested in the beginning who was our -- who would be our commander. We merely wanted to say -- to save our lives. But since there was a company commander, I naturally went to briefings. The first commander was Vujasin, who was commander for a very short while. Then Bandjur, Miroslav Bandjur, succeeded him as a commander. Then I think we requested since in our village we have one or two officers -- army officers who came from our village and who had completed their education. We requested from our commander to have them appointed as our commanders since they used to live there, they still lived there, they were trained there. And Commander Radic who was born in Reljevo, and my last commander was Terzic, who was born in the village of Zabrdje, that is, our village. He was a major. And then Radic, until the end of the war, that is, until after the Dayton Accords, he commanded our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsman, could you please slow down and make breaks. When you told us how the formations came about in the territory of Rajlovac, how the Rajlovac brigade came about, you are telling us about how you organise yourselves, and you said you were attacked -- you said that it was the 8th of May. That is the date when you left your home, your house. Can you tell us whether it was due to some operations of a military unit or why did you leave your area that you lived in?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: I lived in my family house. My wife, my two children, my father, my mother, my brother and I lived in that house. My house was the first one next to Muslim positions. That is, at that time we still did not know that they would be Muslim positions one day. But we watched television. There were already problems in the city after the murder of the Serb member of a wedding party in Bascarsija. And then the attack on Ilidza, on Grbavica. We saw it all on television. We heard all that. And by the 8th of May came to pass, when in an organised and planned attack our well-informed neighbours attacked the entire territory of Rajlovac, and especially the boundary areas along the separation line. And on that day, the 8th of May, there must have been more than 20 shells falling around my house. I managed to carry my two children and with my parents, who are people of advanced age, to pull out of that attack --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I'll stop you now. You are telling us about the separation lines. Between whom and when were those separation lines, partition lines, established?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: The separation lines established by themselves, or shall I say ethnically? Because our whole village, Zabrdje, was an ethnically pure Serb village. Next to us -- next to us our Muslim neighbours were completely leaning against a hill behind us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "leaning against a hill behind us," can you tell us which hill is that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: That hill is called Sokolje, and all along it, that is, its full length is behind our village.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You are telling us about the establishment of ethnic lines, separation lines, and attacks by your neighbours. Can you tell us, did you defend yourselves?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: When that first attack happened, we had absolutely no organisation, nor could we defend ourselves, and we immediately, the same day, drew our, well, so-called line of defence, some three, four hundred metres into -- in the depth -- or into the depth of our territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I gather from your answer that the attackers -- and you tell us that they were your neighbours -- were armed.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you armed too?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and we were armed too. But we only with infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, since as you tell us that territory became the area of responsibility of, say, the Rajlovac Brigade, do you have any knowledge -- can you tell us, how did you arm yourself and how did your neighbours arm themselves? If you know, that is.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Well, we were armed in an identical way, they and we. As you know, near our territory is the Rajlovac barracks. At that time, why, I didn't know anything, which armies, what kind of armies. And we -- from the -- we were issued with weapons from the Rajlovac barracks. That is, we took the weapons from the storage house. And we were issued with -- we took 200 rifles with combat -- complete combat sets, and the Muslims at Sokolje took 800 rifles. I was a witness to that at the Rajlovac barracks when they took that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Please when you tell us that you took your weapons from the barracks in Rajlovac, can you tell us whether it was organised, whether there were personnel in the Rajlovac barracks who issued those weapons to you. Could you clarify this, please.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: I can clarify it -- no, nothing was organised. But the Rajlovac barracks wasn't like other barracks in the city. It wasn't a combat barracks. It was the training ground for cadets and officers who would complete their secondary training there, so there were no conventional soldiers there. And by the date that I'm talking about, everybody had moved already out, including children who were studying there, so that only some of the faculty staff were there, some professors, teachers, and those who could not leave the barracks. So that it was -- well, I won't say it was anarchy, but whoever entered the barracks could pick up a weapon. And whilst I was there, whilst I was present, I know there were six Muslim officers, true, lower-ranking officers, who were also in the barracks, and who had stay there had presumably so they could issue weapons to the Muslims too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sinisa, now, when you tell us that there were Muslims, professional officers, were there also Serbs who were professional officers in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: There were, but very few. I remember the troops -- no, not the troops, because that was not the army. But professors who were officers, they were with their wives. And on the 13th of May, the last -- well, shall I call him an officer? -- left with a convoy and the barracks remained literally, apart from those two, as I said, commanders who were with us, the brigade commanders, the barracks was left without those officers that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "those two brigade commanders who stayed with you," can you tell us if you know where they lived and where did they come from at the time since -- when they were engaged as your brigade commanders? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about Vujasin and Bandjur. I think they just happened to be there when it happened. They were not there a long time there because Commander Radic succeeded them and then Commander Terzic succeeded him in turn.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sinisa, when you tell us that in your area where you lived, that is, the area of Sarajevo, and I'm talking about the area of Rajlovac, ethnic lines were established. Do you have any -- do you know, apart from the infantry weapons that the -- shall I say the adversary side had, and you tell us that they had taken them from the barracks. Were there any other weapons in that area? That is, the line that was established ethnically.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes. As the war progressed, it turned out that the enemy side on the opposite side practically had at their disposal all the weaponry. Throughout the war they fired at us from mortars, from recoilless guns, and they had a tank at that separation line. True, they did not target us directly from the tank. And they also had a gun. I think it was B1. That is, as far as the heavy weaponry they had is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, the Defence should like, in view of the witness's narrative so far -- would like to show the witness the map of the city of Sarajevo so that everybody would be quite clear about which area Mr. Krsman is talking about at a later stage of examination. And with your leave, Mr. Krsman, if you could also draw the separation line about which you say that was ethnically formed in that area after the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic, you may show the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, of course I'm not aware of how much you would like the witness to mark on the map. If it would be a lot, you know that it's sometimes done during the break. If it's just a few lines, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was about to ask that the witness be shown the map because I'd like to ask him a couple of questions, with your leave. But if need be, with your leave, he will mark certain positions, certain places that he said the adversary side acted from.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, about the line that you tell us was ethnically formed in May 1992, did that change?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: As I have told you already, on the 8th of May straight away we left that line moving backward 500 metres, and that is how it was until the 12th of June, 1993. And on the 12th of June, 1993, there was a horrendous Muslim attack so that these lines had to be pulled back another 500 metres almost, almost to -- or, rather, not almost, because we did not retreat any more. We were ready to die old, because otherwise all our families would have been killed, our wives and children, so that that is how they remained until Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, that line which was established in May 1992 to all intents and purposes changed only once, actually, in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the break, I'd like to ask you to draw a line -- or rather, now you draw this first line and then during the break you can also draw the second line, dotted. And since you spoke about positions and the operations of the adversary forces with mortars, you told us, guns, and tanks, I will also ask you to mark those positions during the break and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mark them with a circle. And later on we shall put numbers next to them, because you'll be asked to explain which is which position. But now will you please point at the area that you spoke about and to draw this line which was established in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Can everybody see this on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can pull down the map.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Here. Here. Where it says Bjelice, this is my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we, please, zoom in on where the witness points at. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krsman, when you tell us that it is your house, are you telling us -- are you speaking about the area of a part of Rajlovac where you used to live?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And this is literally the heart of the area of responsibility of my company, but I'll show you that later.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to draw now the line of the area of responsibility of your company during that time. And if you know, I'll also ask you to mark the position of other companies, that is, the established line of separation in May 1992. Use a black marker and draw a line so that we can all be clear what area we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of our battalion -- that is, brigade -- that is, first the brigade and then battalion, was from the Miljacka River to the locality of Bacici. Then straight on to Bozica pump in Brijesce. All of this was held by the 1st Company that was its area of responsibility up to the depot, and then following the tracks -- the rails of the depot, the last pair of rails to Rajlovac. That was the area of responsibility of the 1st Company in the early days of war. Then the 2nd Company was the Rajlovac barracks, all of it, following the inner side of the rail tracks. That is, the position was never across the tracks. And throughout the war, this line never changed. My company, that is, in my village --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, we are talking about the line in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes, in line in May 1992. So the area of responsibility of my line went from the reservoir, the water reservoir supplying the Rajlovac barracks and which was 100 metres away from the road on the Sokolje hill, and the line followed the slope behind -- between us and that, Sokolje. Now, can I now explain. Here you see on the map there's a green area where there are absolutely no indications of houses. Since this is an old map - I don't know how old it is - in this green area, 20.000 people lived. That is, over the past ten years, since 1982 to 1992, 20.000 people settled here. They built their houses illegally. That is why you don't have houses drawn here, as my house is drawn and other houses in Zabrdje.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say 20.000 people since 1982, since you used to live in that area, do you know -- and you are telling us about unlawful settlement -- do you know who is it that came and settled in the area and built houses in that area that you are pointing at on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the relevance is of where these people came from that lived in that part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's relevant in that we want to assess the credibility of the witness, to assess whether the witness is telling the truth, since he said that people settled in that area and that that area, which is indicated by the colour green, he says that 20.000 people lived there. And I think that one should ask whether he knows how this happened, since he's been speaking about unlawful constructions. I wanted the witness to tell us how he knows about this area, about this area that was populated by these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked him where the people came from. If you would say from The Hague -- I mean, it's still not clear to me. But let's just ask the witness to answer and then perhaps keep in mind that just the credibility of a witness should enable us to assess the credibility after he has answered the questions. You may answer the question. The question was where the people came from who unlawfully constructed in that green area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It just so happened that I was on the list of the commission for the census, for the population census in 1991, and I personally listed all those in that local commune. That was a well-known census, in September 1991. It was on that occasion. And these people were on the whole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was before the war; isn't that true? And the question is where --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- The people came from who settled there illegally. Perhaps you are explaining how you know, but perhaps you could first answer the question where they came from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll answer that question immediately. They mostly came from Sandzak, Novi Pazar, Zepa, and the municipality of Visegrad, 90 per cent of them came from those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I don't know whether there's any --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We can have a break. We can have a break. But with your leave, I would like to ask Mr. Krsman to use a black felt-tip to draw a dotted line and indicate in which part that line was changed in June 1992. And with your leave, to mark with a blue felt-tip the positions of the BH army front in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it will then be easier for us to put questions to you later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't it true that blue is always used to mark on request of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In that case, I'll ask the witness to mark the BH army positions, their lines, with a full line and then dots, so that there's a difference between these lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, would you please mark with a dotted line the new line -- your new line established after you were pushed back and then a line -- not just dotted but a dot and then a piece of a line and then a dot again where the BiH formations had their lines. Could you do that during the break. I hope that there will be some time available so that there's a cup of tea or coffee for you as well. But we are very much under a time restraint. Would you be willing to do so during the break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Of course the parties may be present when the witness is drawing these lines. We'll adjourn until twenty minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for marking the map. Could we zoom in a tiny little bit more so that we can copy it on our own maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I see that you have marked with a full line the positions that were such in the month of May. You've marked it with a full black line. Can you tell us what the dotted line, the line with dots, represents.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: It indicates the positions of the BH army, which were opposite our lines, in face of our lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We can see a dotted line in part of the map, which is in the lower part behind the full black line, and in the upper part we can see positions which are above the lines which have -- which consist of a series of dots and then lines. Can you tell us where that is and what these lines, what these lines represent, these interrupted lines, these dotted lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please lower it down a bit.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: So this line indicates the positions that the BH army forced us to adopt on the 12th -- between the 12th and the 13th of June. And in this part of the area of responsibility of the 1st Company, this line is the line that we went to in May, because we weren't able to defend this position in the face of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "in May," can you tell us which year that was exactly?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: We withdrew to this position in May -- we withdrew to these positions here, and the -- didn't change about the four-year period of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to listen carefully to the questions. Because the question was what year, when you were talking about May. You gave an explanation, but you did not mention in what year the month of May the line was changed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood in 1992. I was saying that we established those lines in May 1992, at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, you told us that when you drew the first straight line, you told us about the positions of the Bozica Pumpa and the depot and the Rajlovac barracks. Can you mark on this map the Bozica Pumpa position, the barracks position, the Rajlovac barracks position, and the depot position. If you can, can you make a circle to indicate these positions. For Bozica Pumpa, put "B." For depot, put "D," and for barracks, "B."

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Here on the map you have a sign for Bozica Pumpa. The Bozici lived there. That's the Bozici settlement and that's what this sign indicates.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you could make a circle there.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the depot area that you mentioned on this map.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: This is incorrect on the map. It says the Rajlovac railway station. It's not the railway station. It's the depot. That's where the trains came for servicing and to be washed, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark that with the letter "D."

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the barracks -- you mentioned the barracks. Can you mark the position of the barracks in this area.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: You can see the barracks on the map. It's this complex, the complex consisting of these buildings here, all the buildings in this circle that I have drawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in the depot area, which you have marked with the letter "D" and where it says "Rajlovac railway station," I think you told us that that wasn't a railway station there. And can you mark the position of the railway station, if this is visible on the map.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: The railway station is above this turning from the main road. This is where the railway station was and slow trains were kept there, the local trains, et cetera, that went to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, can you tell us where the command post of your brigade was located?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And I can show it -- I'll mark it with the letter "X." It's in the Rajlovac barracks in the central part of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark this position with "KB" to indicate the command post of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony you said that there were refugees -- Serbian refugees in the barracks who were from parts of Sarajevo. Can you tell us whether from September 1992 up until 1994, did people live in these barracks, women and children? Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Until about the end of May, children lived there too. But after the month of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution objects, again on the grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind the fact that the witness has already said that refugees lived in the barracks, at the beginning of his testimony I only wanted to obtain an answer for the period of 1992/1993, since he has indicated that the command post was located there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness may answer the question. So were there refugees living in the barracks in 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with the exception of children. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You marked the command post of, let's say, the Rajlovac Brigade. Can you now tell us whether you know where the command posts were. Do you know what formation the enemy army had and do you know where their command posts were located?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of formation they had, but I know that the command post was located in the primary school in Brijesce, in the primary school and in the cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the locations -- can you mark the places where the brigade had its command post.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Well, since the names of these streets have been changed -- well, let me just have a look. That's here. That's the Brijesce Street, and that's where the primary school and the cultural centre were located.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You also marked and said what sort of weapons the enemy side had. Can you first of all tell us what sort of weapons you had in your brigade.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: We had -- our company had weapons that a company usually has. And the brigade had the weapons that it needed. We had all the weapons that a brigade usually has. If necessary, I can explain this in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, could you please do so.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: In the company we had machine-guns, 60-millimetre mortars, and 82-millimetre mortars, and we had guns the calibre of which went up to 20 millimetres. We also had artillery support, and the artillery had guns and Howitzers and a tank.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned tanks and guns, and you said that you had support. Can you mark the positions -- did you know where the positions of the tank and the gun were? And if you're able to do so, can you mark these positions on the map.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Well, I didn't want to mark this during the break because the tank and gun fired from where the mosque has been marked on the map. So a gun fired at our positions from here, and there was a tank which was also active but it didn't fire at our positions. It fired on Ilidza because it couldn't fire in our direction since there were -- they were higher up from our position.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you can, can you draw a circle?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: A tank and a gun fired from the same position. A tank appeared when necessary, and a gun was located here. They were very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You've marked these positions and the Bozica pump position and the depot position, can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. I'm a bit confused, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the rest is not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... The witness the positions of his own weaponry. And from his answer, I take it the response was of the weaponry of the other side. So before continuing, will you clarify this issue so that the answer corresponds to what your question was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I asked you about the positions of the weapons that you brigade had, and you said that heavy weapons supported you. Can you mark the tank's position on this map. And if I'm not mistaken, you said that this tank provided support for your brigade. Can you point out the position?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: When I said that we had heavy weapons, heavy weapons provided support for us only when the enemy launched an attack. So we didn't have a tank at a position because tanks don't take up just one position. I thought you were asking me about the tank which was at this position here. But our support -- support provided always when they launched an attack. In about 10 or 15 minutes it arrived at the position and went into action.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, since you were the company commander, can you tell us whether -- or first of all, could you tell us how many men you had in your company.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: At the end of the war, there were 157 men in my company. Naturally the number would vary, as 27 of my men died in my village -- they were killed in my village. That is, village inhabitants died there. I said at the beginning we were issued with about 200 rifles, and there were also invalids. There were wounded people. So there were 157 men at the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as company commander, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the battalion commander, and I received orders from him alone. And a minute ago I mentioned the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you received orders -- all orders from your superior, can you tell us what kind of orders you would receive from your superior.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: All the orders depended on the daily situation. Every morning we went to a briefing -- or rather, to meetings. And depending on the situation, we would receive certain orders. This excludes the standing orders, the daily orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the standard daily orders, what did you mean by that? What sort of orders did this concern? Can you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Well, these orders had to do with not opening fire on -- saving ammunition, or not provoking, monitoring the situation at all times. These were daily orders, and their purpose was to maintain a stable front and not to violate those truces which were signed and which we really never did violate. And it had to do with all the tasks of a combat unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As part of those orders, did you also receive orders that concerned civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Well, in the zone of responsibility of my company, we didn't have any civilian targets. There were just trenches there, men at the front lines. There were no civilians. When we observed the situation, there were no civilians, unless you consider the mosque to be a civilian target. But as there was a tank there and a gun, it was a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that as part of the orders you received on -- and you mentioned daily situations, orders that had to do with the daily situation. What kind of orders were they? Can you explain in a few words what the front where your company was responsible, what was it like? Or if you know anything about the brigade zone or the battalion zone, as you say, what can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Well, our problem was that across the road from us there was a position where the units would always change. The Muslim units would always rotate. Other men would come. And in our positions, the people from our village were there all the time. Whenever the unit changed on their side, they started firing immediately, they started provoking us, and that was a constant problem for us right up until the very end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they provoked you and opened fire, can you clarify that? How often did this occur? And in this zone of responsibility of, let's say, your brigade, were there certain locations where certain -- certain positions where the fighting was more intense? Was there such intense fighting in the zone of responsibility and were there any particular positions which -- at which in your opinion the fighting was more intense or on a larger scale?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: If you have a look at the map and these elevations, you'll see that the entire line of responsibility of our brigade or battalion -- we were in the valley along our line, and the Muslim units were in the hills. And at all times they had the opportunity to fire from an elevated position. And the fact that in my village - it's a small village - the fact that 27 people and 6 women died in my village and over 50 people were wounded, this shows that the fighting was intense on an almost daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, since you marked on this map the positions of both your brigade and positions of the members of the BH army, I will now show you a map on which we have marked positions - of course with the Chamber's leave - and ask you to identify those places on that map, that is, these front lines, and then I'll ask you some questions in relation to that map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, do you recognise the area that we see on this map?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes. This is the blown-up area of the depot, Bozica pump, the Brijesce, and the junction in Brijesce.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
